questions.problem:
Given that ${\int }_{5}^{2}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x=-4$, calculate
${\int }_{2}^{5}(2f(x)+3)\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{5}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{5}^{2}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x=4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can split up the given integral using the sum rule and factor out the constants. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{5}(2f(x)+3)\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{2}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x+3{\int }_{2}^{5}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2(4)+3\cdot x\,{|}_{2}^{5} \\  & =8+3(5-2) \\  & =8+3\cdot 3 \\  & =17.\end{aligned}
$$

${\int }_{0}^{2}(f(x)-5)\,\text{d}x.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{2}^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can split up the given integral using the sum rule and factor out the constants. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}(f(x)-5)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2}f(x)\,\text{d}x-5{\int }_{0}^{2}\text{d}x \\  & =1-5\cdot x\,{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =1-5(2-0) \\  & =1-5\cdot 2 \\  & =-9.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.problem:
Given that ${\int }_{1}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-3$ and ${\int }_{4}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x=8,$ 
then what is ${\int }_{1}^{7}(2-3f(x))\,\text{d}x?$

${\int }_{1}^{7}(2-3f(x))\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
From the adjacent intervals rule, we know that

$$
{\int }_{1}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x\,+\,{\int }_{4}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x\,=\,{\int }_{1}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Plugging in the known information gives

$$
(-3)+8\,=\,{\int }_{1}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x\,⇒\,{\int }_{1}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x=5.
$$

Finally, compute the desired integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{7}(2-3f(x))\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{1}^{7}1\,\text{d}x\,-\,3{\int }_{1}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot x{|}_{1}^{7}\,-\,3(5) \\  & =2(7-1)-15 \\  & =12-15 \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that ${\int }_{3}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x=8$ and ${\int }_{4}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x=4,$ then what is ${\int }_{3}^{6}(5-2f(x))\,\text{d}x?$
questions.worked_solution:
From the adjacent intervals rule, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{3}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{4}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{3}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in the known information into the above gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}8+4 & ={\int }_{3}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ 12 & ={\int }_{3}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute the desired integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{3}^{6}(5-2f(x))\,\text{d}x & =5{\int }_{3}^{6}\text{d}x-2{\int }_{3}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =5\cdot x\,{|}_{3}^{6}-2\cdot 12 \\  & =5(6-3)-24 \\  & =5(3)-24 \\  & =-9.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that ${\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-2$ and ${\int }_{1}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x=3,$ then what is ${\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)+2)\,\text{d}x?$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in the known information into the above gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2+3 & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ 1 & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute the desired integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)+2)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x+2{\int }_{0}^{3}\text{d}x \\  & =1+2\cdot x\,{|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =1+2(3-0) \\  & =1+6 \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Suppose that $f(x)$ is a function such that ${\int }_{8}^{5}3f(x)\,\text{d}x=-2$ and ${\int }_{3}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-3.$ What is the value of ${\int }_{3}^{8}f(x)\,\text{d}x?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's simplify one of the given integrals:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{8}^{5}3f(x)\,\text{d}x & =-2 \\ 3{\int }_{8}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =-2 \\ -3{\int }_{5}^{8}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =-2 \\ {\int }_{5}^{8}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, from the adjacent intervals rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{3}^{8}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{3}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{5}^{8}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-3+\frac{2}{3} \\  & =-\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Definite Integral Using Multiple Properties of Definite Integrals
questions.worked_solution:
Let's simplify one of the given integrals:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-3}^{3}\frac{2}{3}\,g(x)\,\text{d}x & =6 \\ \frac{2}{3}{\int }_{-3}^{3}g(x)\,\text{d}x & =6 \\ {\int }_{-3}^{3}g(x)\,\text{d}x & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Using the adjacent intervals rule and substituting known values, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-3}^{3}(\frac{5}{2}f(x)-4g(x))\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-3}^{-1}(\frac{5}{2}f(x)-4g(x))\,\text{d}x \\  & \,\,\,+{\int }_{-1}^{3}(\frac{5}{2}f(x)-4g(x))\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

By the sum rule for definite integrals,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-3}^{3}(\frac{5}{2}f(x)-4g(x))\,\text{d}x & =\frac{5}{2}{\int }_{-3}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x-4{\int }_{-3}^{3}g(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{2}(-4)-4(9) \\  & =-46.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-3}^{-1}(\frac{5}{2}f(x)-4g(x))\,\text{d}x & =-46-{\int }_{-1}^{3}(\frac{5}{2}f(x)-4g(x))\,\text{d}x \\  & =-46-(-20) \\  & =-26.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Suppose that $g(x)$ is a  function such that  ${\int }_{4}^{8}g(x)\,\text{d}x=5$ and ${\int }_{4}^{1}3g(x)\,\text{d}x=-6.$  What is the value of ${\int }_{1}^{8}g(x)\,\text{d}x?$

Let's simplify one of the given integrals:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{4}^{1}3g(x)\,\text{d}x & =-6 \\ 3{\int }_{4}^{1}g(x)\,\text{d}x & =-6 \\ -3{\int }_{1}^{4}g(x)\,\text{d}x & =-6 \\ {\int }_{1}^{4}g(x)\,\text{d}x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, from the adjacent intervals rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{8}g(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{4}g(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{4}^{8}g(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =2+5 \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Given that ${\displaystyle \int_{0}^{6} \, f(x) \; \textrm d x = -54 },$ what is the value of
${\displaystyle \int_{6}^{0} \bigg( \dfrac 1 3 f(x) + 1 \bigg) \; \textrm d x }?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{6}^{0}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{0}^{6}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x=54\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can split up the given integral using the sum rule and factor out the constants. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{6}^{0}(\frac{1}{3}f(x)+1)\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{6}^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{6}^{0}1\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot 54+x\,{|}_{6}^{0} \\  & =18+(0-6) \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Definite Integral Given Integrals Over Adjacent Intervals
canonical_examples.problem: If $\displaystyle \int_7^{10}f(x)\,\textrm d x = 18$ and $\displaystyle \int_0^{7}f(x)\,\textrm d x = -6$ then what is $\displaystyle \int_0^{10} \big( 2f(x)+1 \big) \,\textrm d x?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
From the adjacent intervals rule, we know that

$$
\int_0^{7}f(x)\,\textrm d x + \displaystyle \int_7^{10}f(x)\,\textrm d x = \displaystyle \int_0^{10}f(x)\,\textrm d x.
$$

Plugging in the known information into the above gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-6+18={\int }_{0}^{10}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ 12={\int }_{0}^{10}f(x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute the desired integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{10}(2f(x)+1)\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{0}^{10}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{10}\text{d}x \\  & =2(12)+x\,{|}_{0}^{10} \\  & =24+(10-0) \\  & =34.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Suppose that $f(x)$ is a  function such that ${\displaystyle \int_4^1 2 \, f(x) \, \textrm dx = -1}$ 
and ${\displaystyle \int_{1}^{-1} f(x) \, \textrm dx = 2}.$  What is the value of ${\displaystyle \int_{-1}^4 f(x) \, \textrm dx}?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's simplify the first given integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{4}^{1}2\,f(x)\,\text{d}x & =-1 \\ 2{\int }_{4}^{1}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x & =-1 \\ -2{\int }_{1}^{4}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x & =-1 \\ {\int }_{1}^{4}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The second integral can be rewritten as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{-1}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =2 \\ -{\int }_{-1}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =2 \\ {\int }_{-1}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, from the adjacent intervals rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-2+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
